_about: Single source of truth for every rendering, and the auditable term ledger (check 5). ONE rendering per referent for the whole book. Before you romanize any name, check here. status per entry: 'attested' (form used in English scholarship, give the citation in note), 'provisional' (your romanization, not found in outside sources), 'decided' (a project style call). If you find a better attested form mid-book, change it here AND grep every built chapter for the old form, then rebuild. Sections are rendered as glossary headings; keys starting with '_' are ignored. Add/rename sections freely (people, organizations, places, terms, ...).

风萧萧.note: The novel's title. It quotes the opening of the parting song sung for the assassin Jing Ke at the Yi River, 风萧萧兮易水寒 (‘the wind whistles, cold runs the Yi’); the note of doomed, high-minded sacrifice governs the book.

徐訏.note: Chinese writer (1908–1980), the novel's author; original name Xu Chuanzong (徐傳琮), pen name Xu Xu. Pinyin form standard in English-language scholarship (older romanization Hsu Yu).

史蒂芬.note: C. L. Stephen, the American naval surgeon; 史蒂芬 transliterates the English name Stephen, restored here.

白苹.note: A dancer at the Paramount, secretly a Chinese agent. Pinyin; 苹 read ping.

梅瀛子.note: A dazzling Eurasian socialite; her father was Chinese (long resident in Japan), her mother American. Pinyin.

海伦.note: Helen Manfield, a shy, music-loving young American. 海伦 = Helen.

曼斐儿.note: Helen's surname; 曼斐儿 transliterates a Western surname whose exact original spelling the source does not give. ‘Manfield’ is a plausible reconstruction.

费利普.note: The surgeon whose clinic Stephen uses; the source spells the name two ways (费利普 and 菲利浦), both transliterating Philip/Phillips.

高.note: Mr. Gao, the Chinese manager of the Weibai Hotel; his American wife and their daughter, Miss Gao, appear at Stephen's party.

莎菲.note: A dancing-girl at the Xiangong; 莎菲 transliterates a Western name (Sophie/Sophy).

铃木次郎.note: A Japanese major general in Mei Yingzi's circle; 铃木次郎 given in its Japanese reading.

山尾本原.note: A Japanese colonel; 山尾本原 read here in a plausible Japanese form, the source giving no romanization.

梅百器.note: Italian conductor and pianist (1878–1946), 梅百器; led the Shanghai Municipal Orchestra 1919–1942 and taught many early Chinese pianists. Helen's teacher.

齐白石.note: Painter (1864–1957), a giant of modern Chinese ink painting.

吴昌硕.note: Painter, calligrapher and seal-carver (1844–1927), a leading figure of the late Shanghai School.

任伯年.note: Painter (1840–1895) of the Shanghai School, noted for figures and birds-and-flowers.

阿美.note: Bai Ping's maid; 阿美, the familiar ‘Ah’ prefix plus Mei.

吉迷.note: Bai Ping's white Persian cat; 吉迷 transliterates a Western pet-name (perhaps ‘Jimmy’), romanized here as Jimi.

陶渊明.note: Poet (365–427), also Tao Qian; the great poet of reclusion and the pastoral in the Chinese tradition.

武则天.note: Empress of the Tang (624–705), the only woman to rule China as emperor in her own right.

西太后.note: Cixi (慈禧, 1835–1908), the Empress Dowager who dominated the late Qing court; the source names her by the palace epithet 西太后, kept here as ‘the Western Empress Dowager.’

宫间登水.note: A Japanese admirer who sends Bai Ping flowers in hospital; the narrator cannot recall the name on the card exactly, so 宫间登水 is given a tentative Japanese reading.

赛金花.note: Celebrated late-Qing courtesan (c. 1872–1936), linked in legend to Field Marshal von Waldersee during the Boxer occupation of Beijing; invoked in ch22 as a byword for a beauty who consorts with the occupier. Pinyin, the standard form.

石涛.note: Monk-painter of the early Qing (1642–c. 1707), a landscapist of the fallen Ming imperial line; a landscape of his hangs in the study in ch23. Pinyin, the standard form.

任堇.note: Painter-calligrapher of the late Qing and early Republic (1881–1936), styled 堇叔 (Jinshu); the digital source prints the corrupt 任董叔 for 任堇叔, emended here (ch23).

本佐次郎.note: A Japanese merchant Mei Yingzi has the narrator take up with (ch25); 本佐次郎 given a tentative Japanese reading, the source offering no romanization.

有田.note: A Japanese colonel (有田大佐, Colonel Arita) at whose Hongkou house the gambling of ch25 takes place; 有田 in its Japanese reading.

武岛.note: A Japanese major general (武岛少将) in the ch25 gambling party; 武岛 in its Japanese reading.

山尾.note: Surname of 山尾少佐, Major Yamao, the officer who forces himself on Helen in ch25; rendered with the same surname form as Yamao Motohara, though the source does not make clear whether the two are the same man.

野村.note: A Japanese colonel (野村大佐, Colonel Nomura) whose car comes for Helen at the end of ch27; 野村 in its standard Japanese reading.

梅武.note: A Japanese rear admiral (梅武少将) of the Navy Ministry, in whose name the Christmas evening party is given (ch29–ch31); 梅武 given a tentative Japanese reading, the source offering no romanization. (少将 is the naval rank of rear admiral.)

陈寂.note: The assumed name the narrator takes when he moves into hiding on Weihaiwei Road (ch26); 陈寂 in pinyin, the given name 寂 meaning ‘silence, stillness, solitude.’

高朗.note: The physician in the white gown at the small private hospital where Stephen dies (ch28), and the hospital’s namesake; 高朗 romanized here (rendered Dr. Gaolang to keep it distinct from Mr. Gao of the Weibai Hotel).

米可.note: A Japanese teahouse hostess and dancer at Umetake's soiree; the source spells her name 米可 and the narrator explicitly notes he cannot tell its nationality, recording only its sound. Rendered as the plausible Japanese given name Miko; provisional, no external attestation.

史托亦夫斯基.note: An elderly White Russian émigré musician Helen meets in Qingdao, who takes her as a pupil and draws her to Beiping (ch39). 史托亦夫斯基 transliterates a Russian surname the source does not give in Latin script; romanized here as Stoyevsky. No external attestation.

福楼拜.note: Gustave Flaubert (1821–1880), French novelist, invoked in the narrator’s Christmas-Eve dream (ch37); the digital source misspells the name as ‘Flaulert.’ See the note at that passage on the unidentifiable ‘holy robe.’

巴哈.note: Johann Sebastian Bach, likened in Helen’s letter to the solemnity of the hills (ch39); 巴哈, the older Chinese form of the composer’s name.

贝多芬.note: Ludwig van Beethoven, likened in Helen’s letter to the grandeur of the sea (ch39); 贝多芬, the standard Chinese rendering.

孟德尔仲.note: Felix Mendelssohn, likened in Helen’s letter to the gentleness of the moonlight (ch39); the source writes 孟德尔仲 for the usual 孟德尔松 (Mengde’ersong), emended in sense here.

工部局乐队.note: The orchestra of the Shanghai Municipal Council (工部局), long led by Mario Paci; in its day the most celebrated orchestra in the Far East.

北京大学.note: Conventional English name of the university; Xu Xu read philosophy there.

百乐门.note: The Paramount Ballroom (百乐门) on Bubbling Well Road, Shanghai's most famous dance hall.

国立艺术院.note: Founded on the West Lake at Hangzhou in 1928 (first president Lin Fengmian); the source calls it simply 艺术院. Rendered by its historical English name.

福源钱庄.note: The traditional Chinese banking house (钱庄, native bank) on which Mei Yingzi's check is drawn in ch22; 福源 romanized as pinyin.

海邻广播电台.note: The Japanese-controlled Shanghai radio station where Helen sings and reads a little English news (ch26); 海邻 (Hailin) transliterates a name not otherwise identified, romanized here.

辣斐德路.note: A street in the French Concession (today Fuxing Middle Road).

静安寺路.note: Major road in the International Settlement, named for the Jing'an (Bubbling Well) Temple; today Nanjing West Road.

麦特赫司脱路.note: A road off Bubbling Well Road (today Taixing Road); the source also spells it 麦特赫斯脱路.

愚园路.note: A road running west from the Jing'an area.

霞飞路.note: The French Concession's main thoroughfare, lined with cafés and shops (today Huaihai Middle Road).

海格路.note: A road on the western edge of the Settlement (today Huashan Road).

善锺路.note: A French Concession street (today Changshu Road); source form 善锺路.

贝当路.note: A French Concession road (today Hengshan Road).

四马路.note: Popular Shanghai nickname (one of the numbered ‘horse roads’) for the settlement's Foochow Road, today Fuzhou Road, known for small restaurants, bookshops and nightlife.

徐家汇.note: District in the southwest of Shanghai (older form Zikawei/Ziccawei), site of the Jesuit St Ignatius Cathedral.

仁济医院.note: A long-established Shanghai hospital (Shanghai's first Western hospital, founded 1844), known to foreigners as the Chinese Hospital or Shantung Road Hospital.

维纳斯.note: A dance hall; 维纳斯 = Venus.

丽都.note: A Shanghai dance hall / entertainment venue.

凯莎舞厅.note: A dance hall; romanization of 凯莎.

立体咖啡馆.note: A café near the corner of Bubbling Well and Medhurst Roads; 立体 means ‘solid’ or ‘three-dimensional’.

大华电影院.note: A Shanghai picture house; 大华 was the Chinese name of the Majestic.

芭口公寓.note: The apartment building where Mrs. Manfield lives; 芭口 transliterates a Western name not identified in the source (pinyin romanization used here).

魏白饭店.note: A hotel managed by Mr. Gao; 魏白 transliterates a Western name not identified in the source.

阿卡第亚.note: A Shanghai dance hall / cabaret of the period; 阿卡第亚 = Arcadia.

仙宫.note: A dance hall where Sophie works; 仙宫 (‘Celestial Palace’), romanized here.

杭州.note: City on the West Lake, southwest of Shanghai; the narrator's old haunt.

西冷饭店.note: A hotel by the West Lake; the source writes 西冷 for 西泠 (Xiling), the name of the district and its famous seal-engravers' society.

金门.note: A restaurant in Shanghai; 金门 (‘Golden Gate’).

锦湘.note: A Chinese restaurant; 锦湘 (the 湘 suggesting Hunan cooking), romanized here.

北四川路.note: A road running north through Hongkou, the Japanese-dominated district north of Suzhou Creek (historically North Szechuen Road).

马斯南路.note: A French Concession street named for the composer Jules Massenet (today Sinan Road).

葛岭.note: Ge Ridge, a hill on the north shore of the West Lake, named for the Daoist alchemist Ge Hong.

苏堤.note: The causeway across the West Lake raised by the poet-governor Su Shi (Su Dongpo).

白堤.note: A causeway on the West Lake, associated with the poet Bai Juyi.

孤山.note: The island hill in the West Lake (孤山, Gushan), famous for plum blossom and the site of the Academy's 1928 opening.

三潭印月.en: the Three Pools Mirroring the Moon
三潭印月.note: A celebrated West Lake scene, an islet ringed by three small stone pagodas standing in the water.

牛公墩.note: A spot on the West Lake named in the source (牛公墩); not securely identified, romanized here.

兆丰公园.note: A large public park in the west of the International Settlement, laid out by the Shanghai Municipal Council in 1914; renamed Zhongshan Park in 1941 for Sun Yat-sen. The novel keeps the older concession-era name Jessfield Park.

汶林路.note: A French Concession street (today Wanping Road), named for J. A. Winling; the Jewish restaurant of Chapter 15 stands at its corner with Avenue Joffre.

姚主教路.note: A French Concession road (today Tianping Road), named for the French Jesuit bishop Prosper Paris (Chinese name 姚宗李, Yao Zongli). The source writes 姚主教路, ‘Bishop Yao’s Road.’

弟弟咖啡店.note: A fashionable café on Avenue Joffre; 弟弟 (‘little brother’) transliterates the English name DD’s. Rendered the DD’s Café in the prose.

天津.note: North China treaty-port city; one of the places Bai Ping speaks of withdrawing to.

浦东.note: The east bank of the Huangpu opposite the Bund; site of a wartime internment camp for Allied nationals.

中西疗养院.note: A Shanghai sanatorium (中西, ‘Chinese-Western’) the narrator suggests for Bai Ping’s convalescence; romanized here.

大西路.note: A road running west out of the International Settlement (today part of Yan'an West Road); the Benner Inn stands off it (ch22).

哥伦比亚路.note: A road in the western external-roads area of Shanghai (today Panyu Road); the Standford gambling-club lane opens off it (ch24).

施高塔路.note: A road in Hongkou (today Shanyin Road), in the Japanese quarter; Colonel Arita's requisitioned house is off it (ch25).

虹口.note: The district north of Suzhou Creek that was the centre of Japanese Shanghai, where the occupying officers are billeted (ch25). Also romanized Hongkew.

槟纳饭店.note: An English-style residential hotel off Great Western Road where Mei Yingzi lodges (ch22); the name Benner Inn is given in Latin letters in the source, on the porcelain lamp-shade and the brass plate.

赛罗凡.note: A fashionable Shanghai restaurant or nightspot named in passing (ch22); 赛罗凡 transliterates a Western name not identified with certainty, rendered here by its sound.

standford.note: A gambling-and-dancing club in a walled lane off Columbia Road, in fact a front for Mei Yingzi's espionage ring (ch24); the name appears in the source only in Latin letters on the neon sign, as standford.

威海卫路.note: A road in the International Settlement (today Weihai Road) where the narrator rents rooms to hide under an assumed name (ch26).

跑马厅.note: The large racecourse of the Shanghai Race Club in the heart of the International Settlement (today the site of People's Park and People's Square); the moon rides above it as they drive down Nanjing Road (ch26).

万国公墓.note: The Shanghai cemetery for the dead of all nations (万国公墓, ‘Cemetery of All Nations’), Chinese and foreign alike, on Hongqiao Road in the western outskirts (founded 1909); Stephen is buried here (ch28–ch29).

静安寺.note: The Jing'an (Bubbling Well) Temple, which gave its name to Bubbling Well Road; the district around it, where the narrator and Helen breakfast (ch29).

马浪路.note: A road in the French Concession officially the Rue Brenier de Montmorand (named 1906 for the French consul-general Brenier; today Madang Road). Shanghai residents shortened it to 马浪路, and the source uses that colloquial form, kept here as Malang Road. Named among the places where the narrator pictures Stephen (ch29).

北平.note: The name borne by Beijing from 1928 to 1949; Helen tells the Japanese she is going to Beiping to return the party invitation (ch29).

汇美饭店.note: The establishment where Mrs. Manfield now works (ch29); 汇美 romanized here, the source giving no Western form.

高叶路.note: The road on which the small private Gaolang Hospital stands (ch28); 高叶路 romanized here. The source names the road 高叶 and the hospital 高朗 (Gaolang); the two forms are kept as printed.

高朗医院.note: A small, clean private hospital on Gaoye Road where Stephen is nursed and dies (ch28); 高朗 romanized here (see Dr. Gaolang).

源裕泰.note: A small, shabby tavern in a lane off Fourth Avenue to which the narrator takes Mei Yingzi (ch31); 源裕泰, a Chinese shop-name, romanized here.

大世界.note: The famous many-storeyed amusement palace at the edge of the French Concession (opened 1917); a dance hall behind it is the scene of ch31.

江湾.note: District in the northern outskirts of Shanghai, site of the Nationalist 'Greater Shanghai Plan' civic centre of the 1930s; under Japanese occupation put to military use. Standard pinyin. Corroborated.

凯第饭店.note: A Shanghai restaurant where the narrator dines alone before the soiree (凯第饭店). No external attestation found; rendered by pinyin, provisional.

白宫舞厅.note: A Shanghai dance hall (白宮舞厅) named by Honsa as a former workplace of one of the officials' wives. Rendered 'the White Palace' (白宮 lit. 'white palace') rather than 'White House' to avoid the American association. Provisional.

青岛.note: Port city on the Shandong peninsula and a noted seaside summer resort; former German (Kiautschou) and Japanese leasehold. Helen winters there (ch38–ch41). Standard pinyin (older ‘Tsingtao’).

国泰.note: The Cathay Theatre (国泰大戏院) on Avenue Joffre, a first-run picture house opened in 1932; where the narrator and Helen see a film (ch43). 国泰 (‘Cathay’) is the house's own Chinese name.

chez Rovere.note: A Western restaurant where the narrator dines with Helen (ch43); the name appears in the source in Latin script as chez Rovere (French, ‘at Rovere's’), kept as printed. No external attestation.

孤岛.note: The name for the foreign-concession enclave of Shanghai between the Japanese occupation of the surrounding city in 1937 and the seizure of the concessions after Pearl Harbor in December 1941, during which the concessions kept a precarious neutral status.

鬼恋.note: Xu Xu's 1937 novella, the work that made his name.

江湖行.note: Xu Xu's later long novel, published 1956–1961; rendered River of Fury in the scholarship of Frederik Green. The Chinese 江湖行 means ‘a journey through the rivers and lakes’ (the itinerant world).

旗袍.note: The close-fitting Chinese woman's dress (旗袍, qipao); ‘cheongsam’ is the established English form used throughout.

月宫.note: The lunar palace of the moon-goddess Chang’e (嫦娥); a figure of cold, remote, solitary beauty, used through Chapter 18 for Mei Yingzi’s radiance and the narrator’s seclusion alike.

寇莉莎.note: An imported drink Mei Yingzi orders (a liqueur or cocktail); the source gives no other identification, so 寇莉莎 is romanized here.

大东亚.note: Shorthand for the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere (大东亚共荣圈), the Japanese imperial propaganda concept proclaimed in 1940. Standard English rendering. Corroborated.
